questions.concept: Slope is a ratio, not an angle
questions.question: A line has slope 2 and another has slope 3. A student says the second is '1 unit steeper in angle.' Why is comparing slopes by subtraction wrong, and what is the real angle gap?
questions.solution: Slope = tan θ, and tangent is NONLINEAR — equal slope steps are not equal angle steps. Slope 2 → θ ≈ 63.4°; slope 3 → θ ≈ 71.6°: a gap of only ~8°, not anything like '1 unit'. Near vertical, tiny angle changes explode the slope (tan 89° ≈ 57). Subtract slopes and you compare rise-per-run, never angles. Convert with arctan first, then subtract — that is the only honest angle arithmetic.

questions.question: Students memorise 'perpendicular slopes multiply to −1' but apply it to vertical/horizontal lines and crash. Prove the rule and state exactly where it breaks.
questions.solution: If two lines make angles θ₁, θ₂ with the x-axis and are perpendicular, θ₂ = θ₁ + 90°. Then m₂ = tan(θ₁+90°) = −cot θ₁ = −1/tan θ₁ = −1/m₁, so m₁·m₂ = −1. It BREAKS when either line is vertical (slope undefined — division by zero) or horizontal paired with vertical (0 × undefined). The product rule needs both slopes finite and nonzero; the vertical/horizontal case must be handled by inspection (x = a ⊥ y = b), not by formula.

questions.question: What does 'the locus of points equidistant from (0,0)' mean — and why does translating that sentence directly into algebra give the circle equation with zero memorisation?
questions.solution: Locus = the set of ALL points satisfying one geometric condition. 'Equidistant (distance r) from origin' translates word-for-word: distance of (x,y) from (0,0) equals r → √(x²+y²) = r → x²+y² = r². No memorisation needed — the equation IS the sentence in symbols. This is the whole method of coordinate geometry: every locus problem is translation, not recall. Condition → distance formula → simplify. Practise reading equations as sentences ('this says every point is 5 from centre') and geometry becomes English.

questions.question: Points A(1,1), B(5,9). A student finds the midpoint ((3,5)) even when asked for the point dividing AB in ratio 1:3. What does the ratio actually control, and what is the correct point?
questions.solution: The ratio controls HOW FAR along the segment you stop: 1:3 means 1 part of the way from A (¼ of the journey), not halfway. Internal division formula: ((m·x₂+n·x₁)/(m+n), …) with m:n = 1:3 → ((1·5+3·1)/4, (1·9+3·1)/4) = (8/4, 12/4) = (2,3). The midpoint formula is just the special case m = n. Mixing them up means ignoring the weights: m pulls toward B, n pulls toward A. Check by distance: AP:PB must equal 1:3 — (2,3) satisfies it, (3,5) gives 1:1.

questions.concept: Why the circle equation is a distance statement
questions.question: Why does (x−h)² + (y−k)² = r² describe a circle, and what breaks if the right side is negative?
questions.solution: The left side is the squared distance from (x, y) to the centre (h, k). Setting it equal to r² says every point is exactly r away — the definition of a circle. If the right side were negative, no squared distance could equal it, so there would be no graph at all: an imaginary circle with a real centre.

questions.question: Why is the product of the slopes of two perpendicular lines exactly −1, and why does a vertical/horizontal pair seem to break the rule?
questions.solution: Rotating a direction vector by 90° maps (1, m) to (−m, 1), whose slope is −1/m — so the product is −1. A vertical line has undefined slope, so the algebraic product cannot be formed; the rule simply does not apply to that pair, and geometrically vertical ⊥ horizontal holds. The exception is about undefined values, not a flaw in the principle.

questions.concept: Why a parabola has a focus and directrix
questions.question: A parabola is defined as points equidistant from a point and a line. Why does this definition produce the familiar y² = 4ax form?
questions.solution: Set distance to focus (a, 0) equal to distance to directrix x = −a: √((x−a)² + y²) = x + a. Squaring and cancelling gives y² = 4ax. The focus–directrix definition is the geometric essence; the standard equation is what it becomes in coordinates. Every conic can be described the same way with an eccentricity, and the parabola is the case e = 1.

questions.concept: Why the distance formula is Pythagoras
questions.question: Why is the distance between (x₁,y₁) and (x₂,y₂) given by √((Δx)² + (Δy)²) and not by adding the differences?
questions.solution: The horizontal and vertical gaps are perpendicular legs of a right triangle, and the straight-line distance is its hypotenuse; the two legs add up to the path along the grid (the taxicab distance), which is longer. Euclidean distance is Pythagoras applied to the coordinate differences. Adding differences measures walking distance, not separation.
